criterion_notes.c1: Examines household wastewater collection, purification, and disposal service delivery — specifically municipal sewer infrastructure provision and mandatory sewer connection versus citizen self-organised onsite sewage facilities (OSSFs) in the Oosterwold residential urban development.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain reading, it examines legal, regulatory, and governance frameworks for wastewater management. Under the narrow rule-type reading, it directly analyses concrete statutory and administrative rules governing household service provision and sewer connection: the statutory municipal sewer duty and mandatory household sewer connection rule (Section 10.33 of the Dutch Environmental Management Act), provincial exemption/waiver requirements and regulatory discretion/non-enforcement, experimental derogation rules under the Crisis and Recovery Act, contractual anterior agreements making self-provision of wastewater infrastructure a prerequisite for residing in Oosterwold, water board discharge permits, pollution vs. sewer treatment levies, compliance inspections, and ownership/provider structure (shifting from public monopoly to individual prosumer OSSFs and back to mandatory public sewer connection).
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative socio-legal empirical case study triangulating doctrinal legal research, systematic document analysis of municipal plans, permits, and land/water agreements, 19 semi-structured key actor interviews (residents, lawyers, policymakers, project members, environmental specialists), and water board inspection monitoring counts of household OSSFs (40 and 199 facilities).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household wastewater service availability, connection mode, and operational reliability/compliance outcomes: absence of public sewer infrastructure initially led nearly all residents to install individual OSSF III units (rather than collective systems), 28 of 40 OSSFs initially and 33 of 199 OSSFs in November 2019 failed discharge permit purification standards (alongside low-flow operational vulnerabilities and water quality deterioration), culminating in a spring 2020 decision to connect future residents and households with inadequate OSSFs to the public sewage system.
criterion_notes.c5: Population/unit of analysis (households/residents and residential plots with OSSFs in Oosterwold, Almere; n=199 OSSFs monitored, n=19 interviewees), legal/regulatory exposure, service/connection and compliance outcomes, and qualitative socio-legal case study design are all clearly reported.

evidence_quotes.quote: The public actors in Oosterwold decided not to install a centralised sewage system. Without a sewage system, the public actors enabled citizens to develop the site incrementally.
The public actors obliged residents to sign an anterior agreement in which residents agree to collect, treat and dispose of wastewater, as a prerequisite for residing in Oosterwold.
The public actors required residents to apply for a discharge permit that was managed by the water board to protect the quality of surface water and to safeguard public health.

Furthermore, 19 key actor interviews served to develop a detailed description of Oosterwold and wastewater management, to cross-check the findings and to identify the experience of the residents and public actors (Weiss 1995).
However, a more recent measurement in November 2019 showed that more than one-quarter of OSSFs (33 of 199) still do not meet the requirements, despite the efforts taken.
From now on, residents who operate an effective OSSF system may keep it; however, future residents and residents with inadequate OSSFs will be connected to the sewage system.

raw_response.exposure: Experimental regulatory shift from centralised municipal sewer provision and mandatory sewer connection (Dutch Environmental Management Act s. 10.33, without a formal provincial waiver) to citizen self-organised wastewater management under the Crisis and Recovery Act, enforced through mandatory anterior agreements as a condition of residence, water board discharge permits, pollution levies, and periodic compliance inspections.
raw_response.outcome: Household wastewater service provision and sewer connection outcomes: absence of public sewer availability and failure of collective self-organisation to emerge, widespread reliance on individual onsite sewage facilities (199 OSSFs installed), persistent operational/purification non-compliance (28 of 40 OSSFs initially and 33 of 199 OSSFs in November 2019 failing permit requirements), surface water quality deterioration, and subsequent regulatory reversal mandating connection to the centralised sewage system for future residents and households with inadequate OSSFs.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Residents/households and residential plots in the Oosterwold urban development, Municipality of Almere, The Netherlands (water board monitoring of 40 initial and 199 November 2019 household onsite sewage facilities; 19 semi-structured interviews with residents, lawyers, policymakers, project members, and environmental specialists, plus 3 pilot interviews and policy/contractual documents).
raw_response.rationale: This qualitative socio-legal empirical case study satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. It investigates how statutory sewer mandates and waiver rules (Dutch Environmental Management Act s. 10.33), Crisis and Recovery Act experimental rules, anterior residency agreements, water board discharge permits, pollution levies, and ownership/provision structures directly governed household wastewater service provision and sewer connection in Oosterwold, Almere. Using doctrinal analysis, municipal/contractual document analysis, 19 semi-structured interviews, and water board monitoring data on 199 household onsite sewage facilities (OSSFs), it documents household reliance on individual OSSFs in the absence of public sewers, high OSSF operational failure/non-compliance (33 of 199 failing standards), and the resulting decision to connect non-compliant and future households to the public sewer network. Per review safeguards, qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are fully eligible for systematic review inclusion.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative socio-legal empirical case study (doctrinal legal analysis, policy/contractual document analysis, 19 semi-structured key actor interviews, and administrative water board monitoring data)
